query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled trace amount of Hf into a eutectic high-entropy alloy, followed by a selective annealing treatment that promotes Hf segregation to lamellar colony boundaries, will form ultra‐thin amorphous intergranular films (AIFs) that blunt crack tips and enhance local plasticity. This modification is expected to simultaneously improve both tensile strength and room-temperature ductility relative to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies exhibiting numerous internal boundaries that act as crack initiation sites under room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a trace addition of Hf during alloy processing and apply a selective annealing treatment optimized to promote Hf segregation to the interphase/colony boundaries.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation; Hf addition must be kept within an optimal concentration window where it effectively segregates without causing excessive interfacial softening or undesired phase precipitation.
generation.structural_mediator: Ultra-thin amorphous intergranular films (AIFs) formed at the lamellar colony and phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The AIFs blunt stress concentrations at the boundaries, delaying crack initiation by absorbing/emitting dislocations and promoting local plasticity, thereby enhancing both strength and ductility without trading one for the other.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to display higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths, along with increased uniform elongation and overall ductility relative to the unmodified baseline.
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that typically suffers from brittle failure initiation at internal boundaries during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.boundary: The positive effects are limited to an optimal range of Hf concentration and processing conditions; below this range, insufficient AIF formation occurs, and above this range, excessive AIF thickness or secondary phase precipitation may lead to interface softening and reduced performance.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal Hf concentration and annealing parameters required to achieve the desired AIF characteristics remain to be determined, as does the quantitative magnitude of the simultaneous strength and ductility improvement.

falsification_experiment.design: Process two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples under identical conditions except that one set receives a controlled trace addition of Hf followed by a selective annealing treatment designed to promote Hf segregation, while the control set does not. Both sets are then subjected to room-temperature tensile testing with in-situ TEM observations to investigate boundary structure evolution.
measurements: TEM imaging of internal boundaries to detect the presence and thickness of AIFs
Fractographic analysis to assess crack initiation and propagation modes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-modified samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the control, or if TEM analysis does not confirm the formation of ultra-thin amorphous intergranular films at the lamellar colony boundaries, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As we all know, the alloying of metals with certain specific elements can very effectively improve alloy properties through various strengthening methods such as precipitation strengthening, solution strengthening, and interface strengthening [,,,]. Hf is an essential alloying element for both the interface strengthening of superalloys and the strengthening of the Ni-Al B2 phase [,,,,,]. Recently, some studies have shown that adding a small amount of Hf to a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy could improve the room-temperature mechanical property of the alloy without significantly reducing the ductility of the alloy through the precipitation of intermetallic compounds such as Ni7Hf2 and Laves phases [,]. However, these studies mainly focus on single-phase high-entropy alloys, and the addition of Hf is relatively large, usually more than one atom. Therefore, the effect of trace Hf addition on the properties of the alloy at room temperature and high temperature is worthy of in-depth investigation.

Damage tolerance is arguably the most important mechanical property of structural materials for many design applications, as it defines the combination of strength and toughness, that is, the ability of a material to resist fracture in the inevitable presence of flaws,,,,. However, in many materials, particularly metallic alloys, toughness comes at the expense of strength. Intrinsic toughness is promoted by extensive plastic deformation, which requires the easy motion and multiplication of dislocations (that can compromise strength), yet contradictorily requires significant hardening to generate strength and ductility by resisting dislocation motion and delaying plastic (necking) instabilities,,. Despite this ‘conflict', the ability to resist cracking in metals and alloys under mechanical loading can be affected by the prevailing modes of plastic deformation and microstructure at the crack tip. Generally, dislocation glide is the primary deformation mechanism at low homologous temperatures in crystalline materials where dislocations move by locally breaking and reforming crystal bonds. chosen.conditions: eutectic high‐entropy alloys processed with an annealing regimen that promotes enrichment of a trace segregant (e.g. Nb) at internal lamellar boundaries, followed by room‐temperature tensile testing
chosen.why: This intervention directly addresses the trade-off in conventional processing (strength vs. ductility) by modifying the weak interphase boundary regions that trigger microcracking. By engineering the boundary chemistry to form a thin, tough interfacial layer, the approach is expected not only to maintain high strength but also to enhance ductility. Its basis in well‐established surface/interface engineering techniques in high-entropy and dual-phase alloys makes it a plausible, testable intervention. The experiment could be falsified if targeted segregant enrichment is not achieved or if the modified alloys do not show improved ductility relative to the unmodified lamellar baseline under room-temperature tensile deformation.

frame.system: Eutectic high-entropy alloys comprising dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal (colony and phase) boundaries that currently nucleate microcracks under tensile loading at room temperature.
frame.goal: Achieve a simultaneous improvement in both tensile strength and ductility at room temperature.
frame.limitation: The existing processing methods increase strength at the expense of ductility by promoting microstructural features (internal boundaries) that foster brittle microcracking, and the wide range of previously proposed design/processing strategies has not overcome the inherent room-temperature brittleness.
root_cause_cues: conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility
constraints: Only a single intervention is allowed
It must improve both strength and ductility without trading one for the other
It should be implementable within the current lamellar-colony baseline without completely overhauling the alloy’s architecture
prior_attempts: Conventional processing that increases strength at the expense of ductility
Multiple microstructural-design and processing strategies aimed at improving the brittle behavior which have overall failed to eliminate room-temperature brittleness
frame.understanding: The intervention should elucidate how a targeted microstructural modification can improve both strength and ductility; specifically, how tailoring the chemistry/structure at internal boundaries can reduce stress concentrations and delay microcrack initiation while simultaneously promoting mechanisms (such as dislocation nucleation or interface sliding) that enhance plasticity.
frame.proposed_hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount of a minor alloying element that segregates selectively to the lamellar colony boundaries to induce the formation of ultra-thin, amorphous intergranular films (AIFs) will both strengthen and toughen the alloy. These AIFs are hypothesized to reduce the local stress concentration at boundaries by blunting crack tips and promoting local plasticity (dislocation absorption/emission) thereby delaying crack initiation and propagation. Relative to the unmodified baseline, the treated alloy should exhibit a higher yield and ultimate tensile strength alongside a significant increase in uniform elongation and overall ductility. The positive effects are expected within a specific segregation range, above which excessive AIF thickness might lead to interface softening, and below which the redistribution of stresses is insufficient. Previous work in nanostructured metals and ceramics has shown that AIFs can significantly improve ductility without sacrificing strength. An experiment to test this hypothesis would involve processing two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples under identical conditions except for the controlled addition of the minor alloying element. Detailed in-situ microscopic observations (e.g., TEM during deformation), along with comprehensive tensile testing at room temperature, would provide the data. If the intervention shows no improvement, or if the alloy demonstrates a further reduction in ductility (e.g., by premature interfacial failure), the hypothesis would be falsified.

decision.trend: The earlier work on eutectic high-entropy alloys has largely focused on manipulating the bulk microstructure through thermomechanical processing and nanostructuring to create dual heterogeneous or ultrafine-grained lamellar architectures. These studies (e.g., PMC6353877 and PMC6687781) achieved impressive combinations of high strength with improved ductility by tailoring the phase distribution and refining the lamellar features. However, while these approaches benefit the overall composite behavior, they have not specifically modified the chemistry and structure of the numerous internal (colony and phase) boundaries where microcracking initiates during room-temperature tensile deformation.
decision.unsolved: The unresolved challenge remains the brittle failure at internal boundaries (lamellar colony edges) which continue to serve as crack initiation sites even when bulk properties are improved. Current strategies lack direct intervention on the interphase boundary chemistry that could mitigate stress concentrations and promote beneficial plasticity mechanisms at these sites.
decision.lever: interphase boundary chemistry via controlled microalloying to induce ultra-thin amorphous intergranular films (AIFs)
decision.why: Building on the trend where bulk microstructural refinements have not fully overcome interfacial brittleness, the most plausible next step is to target the interface directly. By introducing a minor alloying element under conditions (e.g., during a selective annealing stage) that promote its segregation to the lamellar colony boundaries, ultra-thin AIFs can form. These films are expected to blunt crack tips and enhance local plasticity through dislocation absorption/emission. This approach directly addresses the microcracking issue while simultaneously reinforcing the interface, thereby improving both strength and ductility in the existing lamellar-colony baseline.
